I read MENU_AND_HANDHELD_PLAN.md end to end. Stages 1 through 5c are struck through and landed. Stage 5c's closing note is unambiguous: "Nothing. Every read and every write 0008 introduced has a caller, no verb in §7 is without a surface."

The plan then names exactly one thing left, and names it as blocked:

The next thing in this plan is Stage 6, which is not startable … a comment is the first user-generated content in this system and it needs a rate-limiting slice with no menu in it, a REQUIREMENTS.md revision about guest privacy, and a moderation surface.

So progress toward enhancing the menu now runs through the rate-limiting wall, and §17 has been describing that wall — and its fix — in writing for many slices:

the limiter is configured inside AddRestaurantDisplays, and RateLimiterOptions.OnRejected and RejectionStatusCode are single-valued. A second AddRateLimiter call adding a registration policy silently takes over the rejection handler, and a refused registration would then answer with §4.2's "Too many pairing attempts from this device" — worse than no limit, because it is wrong and looks deliberate. Doing it properly means OnRejected dispatching on the endpoint. When it lands, §13 gains the window and permit count beside DISPLAY_PAIRING_*.

I confirmed the wall is real in the source: DisplaysServiceCollectionExtensions.cs sets limiter.OnRejected = WritePairingRejection on the global options, and that handler writes the pairing sentence unconditionally.

What I had designed before hitting the tool limit
M6 Slice 62 — the refusal the endpoint decides, and the limit /register has never had. One behaviour change (registration is rate-limited) plus the mechanism that made it impossible. Findings so far, all verified against the tree:

The dispatch is readable and the fallback is safe. OnRejectedContext.HttpContext.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<EnableRateLimitingAttribute>()?.PolicyName is the same lookup the middleware just did to pick the policy — so when the framework behaves the fallback is unreachable, and when it doesn't the failure mode is a generic sentence rather than a wrong one. That asymmetry is the ruling worth writing down.
A new single owner in src/MyRestaurant.WebApplication/Security/ (that folder exists — ResponseSecurityHeaders.cs, SecurityHeadersMiddleware.cs), enumerating the surfaces so a policy cannot exist without a refusal sentence. DisplayRoutes.PairingRateLimitPolicy moves there (a policy name is not a route or a limit, and it now has a second instance); PairingAttemptsPerWindow/PairingRateLimitWindow stay, because §4.2 states them as properties of the pairing surface.
GenericRefusal as static readonly, not const — so reflection over the type's string literals yields exactly the policy names, and "a policy-name const no policy registers" becomes decidable without keying on a naming convention.
The budget hazard, which I think is the most important thing I found. A per-address partition on /register is not analogous to pairing. Guests on the venue's wifi share one public IP, and UseForwardedHeaders faithfully hands the app that one address — so the whole dining room is one partition. Pairing doesn't care (staff, occasional); registration is bursty and NAT-collapsed. The limit is therefore a volume bound, not a credential bound, and must be sized for a room rather than a person: getting it wrong one way costs spam rows (which F-37 already accepted), the other way costs a seated guest who cannot order. My proposed default is GUEST_REGISTRATION_ATTEMPTS_PER_WINDOW=60 / GUEST_REGISTRATION_WINDOW_MINUTES=10, with a floor that exists to protect guests rather than the server — the inverse of the usual reason for a floor. This is a veto candidate and I want your read before I author it.
Why registration is configurable and pairing is not: §4.2 states 5/minute normatively and there is nothing for an operator to tune; the right registration number is a property of the room, which this project cannot know.
Gate consequences I'd already traced: ConfigurationSurfaceTests derives its key set from FromConfiguration, so the two new keys must land in compose.yaml's web environment mapping, .env.example, and §13's table in the same slice or that gate fails by name. required properties mean RestaurantOptionsTests.Build must change too — and that class has 28 facts and is not cited in §16.4, so the validation facts can go there without moving a census number. The new contract class would take MinimumCountedClasses 34 → 35 with its own §16.4 paragraph.

What I need from you
I stopped at the tool limit partway through enumerating RestaurantOptions construction sites — required properties break every one, and I'd found 40+ files referencing the type without yet separating readers from constructors. I have not authored or packaged anything. Nothing to extract, nothing to delete.

Three things before I write Slice 62:

The observed test count from Slice 61's run — 1283, or something else? Slice 61 explicitly refused to attribute a deviation to itself.
The 60-per-10-minutes default and the shared-egress reasoning — veto now, cheaply, or I build on it.
Confirmation that unblocking Stage 6 is the progress you want, versus the other carried open item (/kitchen has no §16.3 scenario at all, now the largest end-to-end gap). The plan says the rate-limiting slice is the path to the menu; the kitchen scenario is menu-adjacent but doesn't unblock anything.

The census gate caught a real defect in my own work, which is the thing worth reporting. My first insertion of the §16.4 paragraph put a blank line before it but not after, so it fused with the compose-dependency-test paragraph. The gate reported ambiguous: [RateLimitingContractTests.cs, ComposeDependencyContractTests.cs] and the count fell to 33 — my new paragraph uncounted and an existing one knocked out. Fixed and re-run. Still un-run when I stopped: the configuration-surface emulation (my compose.yaml block-boundary matcher was wrong — a script bug, not a tree defect), compose substitution, byte hygiene, and the CS1620/CS4007/@section scans.

What I wrote
New files (three, all needing git add):

Files to delete: none.

The two design decisions worth your veto
One. GenericRefusal is static readonly rather than const. That single keyword is what lets the reflection assertion say every public string constant on this type is a policy instead of every one whose name ends in a word somebody chose. Reverting it to const silently turns that gate into a gate about spelling.

Two — the budget, and this is the real one. GUEST_REGISTRATION_ATTEMPTS_PER_WINDOW=60 / GUEST_REGISTRATION_WINDOW_MINUTES=10, floors 10 and 1. The reasoning is that the partition is a client address and over the tunnel a client address is the whole dining room, so the floor exists to protect guests rather than the server — the inverse of every other bound in §13. To revert: drop both keys from RestaurantOptions, .env.example, compose.yaml and §13's table, delete the GuestRegistrationPolicy entry from RateLimitedSurfaces.All, and remove the @attribute from Register.razor. The mechanism survives that reversion intact — which is deliberate, because the mechanism is F-115 and the policy is not.

Two things I decided without asking
REQUIREMENTS.md gets no revision. Revs 3–6 each added one cross-cutting §8 principle for new intent. A limit on /register is a mechanism catching up to intent §17 already recorded, so this is rev 2's reasoning, not rev 3's. No revision.

Stage 6 is not struck through. It had four prerequisites; this discharges one. The plan now reads one of four discharged and Stage 6a records what landed. Striking it through would claim the stage is startable, and it isn't.

§18 arithmetic — predicted
Where	Tests	Running
Baseline — carried, not measured	—	1283
DisplaysWiringTests (limiter fact moves out)	−1	1282
RateLimitingContractTests (new, 6 facts)	+6	1288
RestaurantOptionsTests (2 facts, 2 theories at 3+2 cases)	+8	1296
§16.3 stays at 21 — no scenario touched. Note the theory arithmetic: 8 tests from 5 attributes, so a run reporting 1293 means the theories collapsed to facts rather than that something failed to compile.

The honest caveat
Nothing was compiled and nothing was run. The largest specific risk is Register.razor: it gained two @using lines and an @attribute whose argument is a member access, and Razor is the most likely place for a compiler-caught error in this tree. Second is that RateLimitedSurfaces referencing both Configuration and Displays namespaces from Security — I did not verify that creates no cycle at the folder convention level, only that it's legal C#.

And one claim no assertion in this slice makes: that a static-SSR Razor endpoint actually carries [EnableRateLimiting] in its endpoint metadata. Everything I asserted is about the list, the lookup and the tree. /display/pair has run on that same unasserted assumption since Slice 22, which is why I recorded it in the plan as carried rather than new — but if it were ever false, both surfaces are unlimited and every test still passes.

So progress toward enhancing the menu now runs through the rate-limiting wall, and §17 has been describing that wall — and its fix — in writing for many slices:

the limiter is configured inside AddRestaurantDisplays, and RateLimiterOptions.OnRejected and RejectionStatusCode are single-valued. A second AddRateLimiter call adding a registration policy silently takes over the rejection handler, and a refused registration would then answer with §4.2's "Too many pairing attempts from this device" — worse than no limit, because it is wrong and looks deliberate. Doing it properly means OnRejected dispatching on the endpoint. When it lands, §13 gains the window and permit count beside DISPLAY_PAIRING_*.

I confirmed the wall is real in the source: DisplaysServiceCollectionExtensions.cs sets limiter.OnRejected = WritePairingRejection on the global options, and that handler writes the pairing sentence unconditionally.

What I had designed before hitting the tool limit
M6 Slice 62 — the refusal the endpoint decides, and the limit /register has never had. One behaviour change (registration is rate-limited) plus the mechanism that made it impossible. Findings so far, all verified against the tree:

The dispatch is readable and the fallback is safe. OnRejectedContext.HttpContext.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata.GetMetadata<EnableRateLimitingAttribute>()?.PolicyName is the same lookup the middleware just did to pick the policy — so when the framework behaves the fallback is unreachable, and when it doesn't the failure mode is a generic sentence rather than a wrong one. That asymmetry is the ruling worth writing down.
A new single owner in src/MyRestaurant.WebApplication/Security/ (that folder exists — ResponseSecurityHeaders.cs, SecurityHeadersMiddleware.cs), enumerating the surfaces so a policy cannot exist without a refusal sentence. DisplayRoutes.PairingRateLimitPolicy moves there (a policy name is not a route or a limit, and it now has a second instance); PairingAttemptsPerWindow/PairingRateLimitWindow stay, because §4.2 states them as properties of the pairing surface.
GenericRefusal as static readonly, not const — so reflection over the type's string literals yields exactly the policy names, and "a policy-name const no policy registers" becomes decidable without keying on a naming convention.
The budget hazard, which I think is the most important thing I found. A per-address partition on /register is not analogous to pairing. Guests on the venue's wifi share one public IP, and UseForwardedHeaders faithfully hands the app that one address — so the whole dining room is one partition. Pairing doesn't care (staff, occasional); registration is bursty and NAT-collapsed. The limit is therefore a volume bound, not a credential bound, and must be sized for a room rather than a person: getting it wrong one way costs spam rows (which F-37 already accepted), the other way costs a seated guest who cannot order. My proposed default is GUEST_REGISTRATION_ATTEMPTS_PER_WINDOW=60 / GUEST_REGISTRATION_WINDOW_MINUTES=10, with a floor that exists to protect guests rather than the server — the inverse of the usual reason for a floor. This is a veto candidate and I want your read before I author it.
Why registration is configurable and pairing is not: §4.2 states 5/minute normatively and there is nothing for an operator to tune; the right registration number is a property of the room, which this project cannot know.
Gate consequences I'd already traced: ConfigurationSurfaceTests derives its key set from FromConfiguration, so the two new keys must land in compose.yaml's web environment mapping, .env.example, and §13's table in the same slice or that gate fails by name. required properties mean RestaurantOptionsTests.Build must change too — and that class has 28 facts and is not cited in §16.4, so the validation facts can go there without moving a census number. The new contract class would take MinimumCountedClasses 34 → 35 with its own §16.4 paragraph.

The two design decisions worth your veto
One. GenericRefusal is static readonly rather than const. That single keyword is what lets the reflection assertion say every public string constant on this type is a policy instead of every one whose name ends in a word somebody chose. Reverting it to const silently turns that gate into a gate about spelling.

Two — the budget, and this is the real one. GUEST_REGISTRATION_ATTEMPTS_PER_WINDOW=60 / GUEST_REGISTRATION_WINDOW_MINUTES=10, floors 10 and 1. The reasoning is that the partition is a client address and over the tunnel a client address is the whole dining room, so the floor exists to protect guests rather than the server — the inverse of every other bound in §13. To revert: drop both keys from RestaurantOptions, .env.example, compose.yaml and §13's table, delete the GuestRegistrationPolicy entry from RateLimitedSurfaces.All, and remove the @attribute from Register.razor. The mechanism survives that reversion intact — which is deliberate, because the mechanism is F-115 and the policy is not.
